doc.title: Konitz Lee — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Konitz-Marsh Atlantic session with Pettiford and Clarke
summary: He felt uncomfortable on the session, tells of Oscar Pettiford, and a gig in his band.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Big band discipline versus small-group freedom

blocks.x: I want to ask you about all of those things shortly because I have questions about all of those. What about the date three days after the “Confucius”, with you, Warne, Sal Mosca, Billy Bauer, Oscar Pettiford, and Kenny Clarke? How did you feel about that one?

I was very uncomfortable in that situation also because [of] the smoking that [was] inevitably involved in those days. I don’t think I smoked that day and I think Sal and Warne were well “fortified” and somehow you can’t penetrate that kind of structure too easily.
Well again that’s considered one of your landmark records and I know lots of people who love the way that you and Warne played on that.

Some of it’s nice but just over all it was a feeling . . . of not being comfortable with anybody there, really. Not Oscar or Kenny. Kenny was always cool but Oscar was a difficult man for me although I played in his little band briefly.

I don’t know how big it was but we played a little club in the forties in midtown Manhattan and he had an arrangement of one tune . . . ”Passion Flower” or something like that and Johnny [Hodges] came in I remember and I think I played it an octave higher or something. I didn’t know what to do with it. But anyway I sometimes closed up shop and that’s one of the times I closed up. I’m grateful that something remains but for the most part these days they’re all joyous experiences.
